The Examiner rejects claims 1-2, 5-10, 12-15, 17-21, and 23 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada et al. (USPA 2007/0055163, hereinafter Asada) and Banet et al. (USPA 2017/0188973, hereinafter Banet).
The applicants respectfully traverse this rejection.
1. Asada purposely teaches the elimination of the AC component of the PPG signal in the determination of a user's blood pressure.

The applicants specifically claim extracting information regarding a blood volume pulse from the AC component of the output signal of a PPG sensor, and using this extracted AC component to determine the user's blood pressure.
Asada specifically teaches techniques for eliminating the effects of the AC
component when determining the user's blood pressure.
In response to the applicants' argument that Asada purposely ignores the AC component of the PPG signal, the Examiner asserts:
"While Applicant asserts that Asada teaches that the PPG/ABP relationship is

complicated by oscillations such as rhythmic variations, Asada does not specifically teach against using such rhythmic variations. A simplification of a complex relationship does not remove the motivation to utilize the advantages of the complex relationship. Although the PPG/ABP blood pressure may be complicated by microcirculatory oscillations, a higher complexity does not preclude advantages that would arise from using an AC portion of the PPG signal.
For the sake of advancing prosecution, Examiner has presented further evidence
which teaches the amended limitation of an AC component.
"As noted in the rejection of claim 1, additionally or alternatively, Asada may

still read upon extracting information from an AC component, since Asada first extracts an original waveform having AC components and then applies an averaging to process information therefrom; an average of an AC component is
still extracted information from an AC component.
"Furthermore, Asada's removal of rhythmic oscillations may not read upon

removal of an AC component, which Applicant contends that Asada is performing. It is commonly-known in the art that the term "AC component," when referring to a pulse plethysmograph signal, typically refers to the waveform containing typical indications of systole, diastole, and dicrotic notches (what first comes to mind when viewing a PPG waveform), where it appears that Asada's processing is to remove motion noise." (Office action, page 13, line 14 - page
14, line 8.)
These assertions are clearly erroneous.
As noted in the applicants' prior response, Asada specifically teaches using the
peak amplitude of the PPG waveform to determine the blood pressure.
"The blood pressure measurement device has a processor that receives the
plethysmographic signals from the sensor and derives an arterial pressure from
the value of externally applied pressure and the height at which a peak
plethysmographic signal is obtained" (Asada [0015], emphasis added.)
Asada's FIG. 4C clearly illustrates Asada's determination of the maximum PPG signal amplitude at 414, then calculating the ABP (Arterial Blood Pressure) based on this maximum/peak PPG signal at 416.
"Once the PPG signal amplitudes are measured the peak PPG amplitude is
determined 414. Like the calibration method above, spurious data points and
oscillations between beats of the heart SVG {EMBED HERE} 2.212.827 may be removed from the peak 41 plethysmographic signal amplitude. If the PPG signal has a peak at the

transmural height, then the ABP is 41
equal to the previously calibrated MAP.

However, if the peak PPG signal is at a different height, then the ABP is equal 41
to the constant external pressure applied to the extremity plus the

hydrostatic pressure, which can be 41
found by solving Eqn. 4 with the new height 416." (Asada [0076], emphasis FIG. 4C SVG {EMBED HERE} 0.2330.09 8
added.)

The AC component of the PPG signal corresponds to the changing volume of blood for each pulse of the user's heart. Asada specifically teaches techniques for removing this AC component from the PPG signal to improve the process of determining peak values of the PPG signal.

The terms "AC component" of a signal and "peak" of a signal are terms of the art in signal processing, with very specific meanings. Below is a copy of a part of Asada's FIG. 3, with annotations added by the applicants to identify the AC component and peak values of Asada's PPG signal.

As is clearly evident, although related to the same signal, the signal's peak value is different from the signal's AC component. Most significantly, the peak value provides no information regarding the AC component, and the AC component provides no information regarding the peak value. When Asada processes the signal to determine the peak amplitudes, all information regarding the AC component of the signal is lost.

The applicants disclose using the AC component to determine blood pressure, whereas Asada uses the peak value to determine blood pressure. The difference between these two approaches is illustrated using a portion of Asada's signal between points identified as 'Peak 1' and
substantially equal.
Of particular note, peak 1 is measured at a first height (height 1) relative to the

user's heart, and peak 2 is measured at a second height (height 2), and the difference in hydrostatic pressure at these two heights account for the different peak values. Asada relies on determining the differences between peak values at different heights to compensate for the particular height of the PPG sensor when the blood pressure is being measured.

Pr =p-g-h + wherein, p is the density of the blood, g is the acceleration of gravity, and h is the height offset of the measurement site relative to the proximal aorta. Thus, with the known PPG sensor unit pressure and hydrostatic pressure the
ABP can be found." (Asada [0075], emphasis added.)

Because, as illustrated above, the AC components at height 1 and height 2 are substantially equal, if Asada used the AC components, as proposed by the Examiner, it would be impossible for Asada to perform its primary task of compensating the blood pressure readings to account for different PPG sensor heights.

Further, the Examiner's assertion that "Asada may still read upon extracting information from an AC component, since Asada first extracts an original waveform having AC components and then applies an averaging to process information therefrom; an average of an AC component is still extracted information from an AC component", cited above, is misleading, and incorrect.
The Examiner omits the critical step of Asada wherein between Asada's

extraction of "the original waveform having AC components" and Asada's application of "an averaging process", Asada specifically teaches determining the peak values of the PPG signal. It is these peak values that are averaged, and not the AC components, as asserted by the Examiner.
2. Asada effectively teaches against using the AC component of the PPG signal in the determination of the user's blood pressure.
The applicants note that Asada specifically discloses the advantages that are
obtained by eliminating the AC component of the PPG signal from the determination of the user's blood pressure, in addition to the benefits of using the peak of the PPG signal.
Specifically, Asada discloses that the AC component of the PPG signal
introduces spurious data points, which, by definition of 'spurious', means undesirable signals that will adversely affect the intended determination of an accurate blood pressure determination.
"PPG amplitude measurements are obtained by applying a peak detection

algorithm to each calibration data set. Once the beat-by-beat amplitudes are calculated, spurious data points are removed by applying a 3-element moving window median filter to the data. The PPG/ABP relationship is complicated by oscillations such as rhythmic variations in microcirculatory blood volume.

A moving window averaging is performed to eliminate oscillations between several beats, but other signal processing alternatives exist, including band-pass filtering or fitting a spline, as methods of removing PPG baseline oscillations that are not directly due to oscillations in the ABP, and any such signal processing is
within the scope of the present invention." (Asada [0068], emphasis added.]
"Like the calibration method above, spurious data points and oscillations
between beats of the heart may be removed from the peak plethysmographic
signal amplitude." (Asada [0076], emphasis added.)
The applicants respectfully maintain that Asada's teaching of the need to

eliminate variations reflected in the AC component of the PPG signal in the determination of a more accurate / less noisy blood pressure measurement necessarily implies that Asada teaches against including the AC component of the PPG signal in the determination of a user's blood pressure.
3. There is no apparent reason to combine Asada and Banet.
The Examiner asserts:
"Asada does not explicitly teach the invention wherein information is extracted
regarding a blood volume pulse from an AC component of an output signal of the
PPG sensor.
"Banet teaches the invention wherein information is extracted regarding a
blood volume pulse from an AC component of an output signal of the PPG sensor (Paragraph 0106: application of pressure to identify AC components). Banet
teaches analogous art in the technology of PPG waveform analysis (Abstract).
"It would have been obvious to one having skill in the art before the effective

filing date to have modified Asada in view of Banet to include extracting information from an AC component of the output of the PPG sensor, the motivation being that it is well-known that the maximum amplitude of the
pulsations corresponds to an applied pressure equal to mean arterial pressure
(MAP)." (Office action, page 5, lines 13-22.)
The applicants respectfully disagree with this assertion.
As detailed above, Asada specifically uses the peak signal amplitude to

determine the user's blood pressure, because the peak signal amplitude varies with the height of the PPG sensor relative to the user's height, and a more accurate blood pressure reading can be obtained by adjusting the measured pressure to compensate for different PPG sensor heights when in use. As also detailed above, the use of the AC component of the signal in lieu of the peak of the signal precludes this ability in Asada, rendering it unsuitable for its intended purpose.
The Examiner's attention is requested to MPEP 2143, wherein it is stated (emphasis added):
"If the proposed modification would render the prior art invention being modified unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, then there is no suggestion or
motivation to make the proposed modification."

In like manner, there is no apparent reason to 'add' Banet's AC component based method of determining blood pressure to Asada's peak signal method of determining blood pressure, because there is no apparent benefit to be obtained by such an addition. As the Examiner notes, "it is well-known that the maximum amplitude of the pulsations corresponds to an applied pressure equal to mean arterial pressure", and this is what Asada teaches.

Because there is no apparent reason to combine Asada and Banet in the manner proposed by the Examiner, and because Asada effectively teaches against the inclusion of the AC component of the PPG signal in the determination of a user's blood pressure, the applicants respectfully maintain that the rejection of claims 1-2, 5-10, 12-15, 17-21, and 23 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada is unfounded, and should be withdrawn.
The Examiner rejects claims 16 and 22 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada, Banet, and McEwen et al. (USPA 2009/0124912).
